paper_metadata.title: A performance characterization of quantum generative models

summary: This paper benchmarks QCBM and QGAN generative models on 2D and 3D synthetic/financial datasets using Qiskit and PennyLane state-vector simulators. The best reported quantum result is KL = 0.029 on the 3D X dataset with the discrete copula architecture, while classical GANs remain competitive and sometimes better; the authors explicitly state that the experiments do not demonstrate quantum advantage.

experiments.description: Benchmark of quantum circuit Born machines (QCBM) for learning low-dimensional synthetic and real financial distributions using continuous, discrete standard, and discrete copula circuit architectures under min-max normalization or PIT preprocessing.

algorithm.variant: QCBM (continuous, discrete standard, and discrete copula architectures)
algorithm.ansatz: data-reuploading continuous circuit; discrete variational circuit; copula-structured discrete circuit
algorithm.convergence_criteria: maximum training epochs or when change in KL divergence between successive steps drops below a threshold (threshold not specified)

hyperparameters.continuous_architecture_shots: state-vector exact expectation values used; no shot sampling in simulation

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Subsequent circuit blocks initialized from previously fitted parameters; new blocks initialized to zero / identity. For the first block, initialization not specified.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Discrete architectures discretize each data dimension into 16 bins using 4 qubits per dimension; continuous architecture uses one qubit per data dimension and outputs expectation values of Pauli-Z observables normalized to [0,1].
problem_formulation.objective_function: Minimize KL divergence between empirical data histogram Q and model distribution P(θ): arg min_θ C_KL(Q,P(θ))
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: PIT preprocessing for copula architecture; no explicit penalty terms

problem_instance.description: Learning synthetic 2D/3D distributions and real stock-return distributions.
problem_instance.dataset_name: mixture of Gaussian distributions, X-shaped distribution, O-shaped distribution, stocks

dataset_specification.stocks: Yahoo Finance daily close prices converted to daily returns; 2D and 3D versions used

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Either min-max normalization to [0,1] or probability integral transform (PIT) to learn copulas; PIT computed from sampled histograms.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Five independent runs per configuration; report minimum KL over runs and average KL curves with standard deviation.

implementation_details.code_url: open-sourced simulation library qugen (URL not provided in excerpt)
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: min-max normalization or PIT; histogramming of data for KL computation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sample generation from trained circuit; KL divergence evaluation

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: generally decreasing with depth/epochs; discrete copula with PIT often more stable

speedup_claims.factor: up to two orders of magnitude fewer parameters
speedup_claims.conditions: for some 2D/3D datasets, especially O and X distributions, when comparing parameter counts needed to reach similar KL divergence
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a parameter-efficiency claim, not a wall-clock speedup; experiments were run on state-vector simulators, not gate-based QPU hardware.

speedup_claims.factor: lower runtime per sample for discrete copula than other discrete variants
speedup_claims.conditions: resource estimates on quantum hardware; depends on data dimension d, discretization r, and number of blocks Nb
speedup_claims.caveats: Derived from resource formulas, not measured on hardware.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Resource scaling linear in data dimension d for all architectures; discrete copula has lower asymptotic runtime per sample than other discrete variants
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: Table III gives runtime/sample scaling: continuous Ns Nb(d+4); discrete standard Nb(rd+2); discrete copula r(d-1)+1 + Nb(r(r-1)/2 + 3)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: No crossover size established; only simulator benchmarks on 2D/3D toy and small real-finance datasets.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Up to 12 qubits for discrete 3D circuits; continuous circuits use 2-3 qubits. Best reported quantum results are parameter-efficient, e.g. 3D X with discrete copula QGAN/QCBM at KL 0.029 using 54-162 parameters, but this is not a hardware advantage demonstration.
limiting_factors: All experiments are state-vector simulations, not QPU runs
Classical baselines are competitive or better on several datasets
Advantage is only parameter-efficiency on low-dimensional benchmarks

notes: Paper explicitly states all experiments were run on Qiskit and PennyLane state-vector simulators.
No gate-based QPU hardware was used; all quantum resources are simulation-based.
The paper reports resource formulas and qubit counts, but not a single fixed circuit depth because depth varies with the number of blocks.
The paper does not claim asymptotic quantum speedup; it reports empirical parameter-efficiency advantages only.
The paper reports that quantum models sometimes need fewer parameters than classical neural networks, but it explicitly states that the experiments do not demonstrate quantum advantage.
Classical GANs achieve comparable or better KL on several datasets, especially at similar parameter counts.

experiments.description: Benchmark of quantum generative adversarial networks (QGANs) with a quantum generator and classical discriminator for the same low-dimensional synthetic and real financial datasets, comparing continuous, discrete standard, and discrete copula architectures under min-max or PIT preprocessing.

algorithm.variant: QGAN with quantum generator and classical discriminator; continuous, discrete standard, and discrete copula variants
algorithm.ansatz: data-reuploading continuous circuit; discrete variational circuit; copula-structured discrete circuit
algorithm.optimizer: gradient descent; Optax/JAX for continuous, parameter-shift-based gradient descent for discrete
algorithm.convergence_criteria: training for a fixed number of epochs; no explicit universal stopping threshold reported

activation_functions.discrete: leaky ReLU hidden layer, sigmoid output

hyperparameters.epochs: varies by dataset and architecture; figures show up to 500, 1000, 2000, 10000 depending on case

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Cold-started all QGANs; no warm-start from lower-depth circuits. Exact initial parameter distribution not specified.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Discrete architectures use 4 qubits per dimension; continuous architecture uses one qubit per dimension and outputs expectation values. QGAN generator samples are fed to a classical discriminator.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Adversarial training with generator loss LG = -1/m Σ log D(s(θ)) and discriminator loss LD = -1/m Σ [log D(x) + log(1-D(s(θ)))]
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: PIT preprocessing for copula architecture; no explicit penalty terms

problem_instance.description: Learning synthetic 2D/3D distributions and real stock-return distributions with adversarial training.
problem_instance.dataset_name: mixture of Gaussian distributions, X-shaped distribution, O-shaped distribution, stocks

dataset_specification.stocks: Yahoo Finance daily close prices converted to daily returns; 2D and 3D versions used

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Min-max normalization or PIT; PIT used to match discrete copula architecture.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Five independent runs per configuration; KL divergence tracked over epochs and minimum KL reported.

implementation_details.code_url: open-sourced simulation library qugen (URL not provided in excerpt)
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: min-max normalization or PIT; discriminator input formatting for continuous vs discrete cases
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: sample generation from trained generator; KL divergence evaluation

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: generally decreasing; discrete copula with PIT often more stable and less prone to sudden jumps

speedup_claims.conditions: same datasets and preprocessing; based on minimum KL over runs
speedup_claims.caveats: Difference is smaller than architecture/normalization effects; no wall-clock speedup shown.

speedup_claims.factor: up to two orders of magnitude fewer parameters
speedup_claims.conditions: for some 2D/3D datasets, especially O and X distributions, when comparing parameter counts needed to reach similar KL divergence
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a parameter-efficiency claim, not a wall-clock speedup; experiments were run on state-vector simulators, not gate-based QPU hardware.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Resource scaling linear in data dimension d for all architectures; discrete copula has lower asymptotic runtime per sample than other discrete variants
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: Table III gives runtime/sample scaling: continuous Ns Nb(d+4); discrete standard Nb(rd+2); discrete copula r(d-1)+1 + Nb(r(r-1)/2 + 3)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: No crossover size established; only simulator benchmarks on 2D/3D toy and small real-finance datasets.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Up to 12 qubits for discrete 3D circuits; continuous circuits use 2-3 qubits. Best reported QGAN result is 3D X with discrete copula PIT at KL 0.029 using 54 parameters.
limiting_factors: All experiments are state-vector simulations, not QPU runs
Classical baselines are competitive or better on several datasets
Advantage is only parameter-efficiency on low-dimensional benchmarks

notes: Paper explicitly states all QGAN experiments were simulated on classical computers using state-vector simulation and classical optimization.
No gate-based QPU hardware was used; the discriminator is classical and only the generator is quantum.
The paper reports resource formulas and qubit counts, but not a single fixed circuit depth because depth varies with the number of blocks.
The paper does not claim asymptotic quantum speedup; it reports empirical parameter-efficiency advantages only.
The paper says QGANs can outperform QCBMs in some cases and can be parameter-efficient, but it does not claim a demonstrated practical quantum advantage.
The strongest results are on low-dimensional synthetic data, not a meaningful industrial-scale problem.
